summaries.example: Imagine that a ball rolls toward a toy car and the car moves. Most people say the ball caused the car to move. An occasionalist gives a different explanation: the ball’s arrival is an occasion, or signal, for God to bring about the car’s movement. The ball is not the true cause. God is.
summaries.summary: Occasionalism is a theory about causation, or about how events bring about other events. Everyday experience suggests that things cause one another: a hand moves a cup, fire heats water, or one ball moves another. Occasionalists challenge this picture. In the strongest version, called global occasionalism, God is the only genuine cause. Created things do not truly produce effects. They are at most occasional causes: when a created event happens, God acts in a regular way to bring about the next event. Some philosophers defended a weaker, local version. They claimed that God is the only true cause in a particular area, such as interactions between bodies, while other created causes may be real. The entry follows this idea through several traditions. Islamic thinkers, including al-Ash‘ari and al-Ghazali, examined whether created causes could have powers that would limit divine power or make miracles impossible. Later, philosophers in medieval Christian Europe and early modern Europe debated similar questions. Descartes’s position is disputed, while several Cartesians, especially Nicolas Malebranche, defended forms of occasionalism. George Berkeley denied causal power to physical objects but treated spirits differently. The debate also compares occasionalism with other views: conservationism gives creatures genuine causal activity while God preserves them, and concurrentism says God and creatures directly cause an effect together. Occasionalism instead gives causal activity entirely to God within the relevant domain.
key_ideas: We often see one event followed by another and call the first event a cause.
Occasionalists say that God is the only true cause, either everywhere or only in a certain area.
Created things, such as bodies, may be occasions: their actions regularly go along with effects, but they do not produce those effects by themselves.
Different philosophers defended different versions of occasionalism. Some allowed created minds or other things to have limited causal powers.
The view grew in Islamic philosophy and theology and later appeared in medieval Christian and early modern European philosophy.
Berkeley agreed that physical objects are not true causes, but he held that minds or spirits are active in ways that raise further questions.
summaries.why_it_matters: Occasionalism asks a basic question: when one event follows another, what does it mean to say that the first caused the second? It also explores how religious ideas about God’s power fit with ordinary explanations of nature. The theory helps us see that regular patterns, such as fire being followed by heat, can be explained in more than one way. It also shows why philosophers distinguish what we observe from what they think is happening underneath those observations.

important_terms.definition: The idea that, in some area of events, God is the only true cause and created things are only occasions for what happens.
Something that seems to help bring about an event but is not its real cause. It is an occasion for God to act.
A power that really brings about an effect, according to the view being discussed.
A connection in which one event must produce another. Occasionalists question whether created things have connections this strong.

questions_to_think_about: If a button is pressed and a bell rings, what makes the button a cause rather than merely something that comes first?
Could events happen regularly even if the first event were not the true cause?
Does a miracle require the usual pattern of nature to be necessary?
Which seems more convincing: created things causing events, or God causing events when created things provide occasions?

summaries.example: Suppose a person wills to raise an arm, and the arm rises. A common explanation says the mental act causes bodily motion. Malebranche’s occasionalism rejects this as genuine causation: the person’s volition is an occasion, while God directly produces the bodily change according to a general law linking mind and body. A divine concurrentist would instead say that God and the person both contribute directly to the event. The disagreement is not about whether the arm rises regularly, but about what kind of causal power the person possesses.
summaries.summary: Occasionalism is a metaphysics of causation that denies that created things are genuine causes within a specified domain. Its central claim is that God alone possesses the kind of causal power that truly produces effects. Created events may still be important: they are occasional causes, events that regularly provide the circumstances in which God brings about another event. Thus occasionalism does not reject the regularity of nature. It gives that regularity a different foundation, namely God’s general volitions or laws, rather than necessary powers belonging to created natures. The view has both global and local forms. Global occasionalism denies genuine causation to all finite substances. Local occasionalism restricts the denial to a domain, such as bodily interactions, while allowing genuine causes elsewhere. The historical discussion begins with Islamic occasionalism. Al-Ghazali criticized an Aristotelian picture on which created natures contain causally necessitating powers, partly because such a picture appeared to threaten divine omnipotence and the possibility of miracles. Scholars disagree about whether his own position was fully occasionalist or left room for secondary causation. In medieval Christian Europe, Nicholas of Autrecourt criticized claims to know necessary causal connections, but his skeptical project does not clearly make him an occasionalist. Early modern Cartesians developed several versions: Descartes’s own view is disputed, while La Forge, Cordemoy, Clauberg, and Geulincx differed over which domains lacked creaturely efficacy. Malebranche offered especially extensive defenses. His arguments appeal to the passivity of bodies, limits on an agent’s knowledge of its effects, the absence of necessary connections between created causes and effects,,
key_ideas: Occasionalism distinguishes genuine causation from occasional causation rather than treating every regular sequence as one kind of causal relation.
Its scope can be global or local. The entry therefore does not treat every philosopher labeled an occasionalist as holding the same thesis.
The debate concerns both natural causation and divine action: if God is the ultimate source of existence, what causal work remains for creatures?
Malebranche’s arguments include the passive-nature argument, the no-knowledge argument, the no-necessary-connection argument, and the continuous-creation argument.

The no-necessary-connection argument challenges the claim that creaturely natures entail their effects. The continuous-creation argument instead focuses on the relation between God’s conserving and creating activity.

Occasionalism differs from Leibniz’s pre-established harmony. Both reject causal interaction between distinct finite substances, but Leibniz allows substances to cause changes within themselves, whereas Malebranche denies creaturely causal power more broadly.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory matters because it separates three questions that are often run together: whether events occur regularly, whether one event produces another, and whether God’s activity is compatible with creaturely causation. It also provides a framework for comparing major theories of divine action. Conservationism, concurrentism, pre-established harmony, and occasionalism agree on some dependence of creatures on God but assign causal activity differently. The arguments remain philosophically useful because they test whether causation requires necessity, whether regularity can have a theological foundation, and whether the possibility of divine intervention is compatible with stable natural laws

important_terms.definition: A metaphysical theory according to which God is the unique genuine cause within a specified domain, while alleged creaturely causes are at most occasions for divine action.
The strongest form of occasionalism: all causation by finite or created things is denied, and divine causation alone is genuine.
A restricted form of occasionalism in which creaturely causation is denied only in a particular domain, while some created causes remain genuine elsewhere.
A cause that does not produce its effect but occasions God’s regular, law-like activity linking one event type with another.
The view that created substances retain their causal powers while God preserves them in existence; God’s role in ordinary effects is indirect.
The view that God and a creature are both immediate causes of a natural effect, so divine and creaturely causation operate together.
A relation in which a cause necessarily produces its effect. Malebranche treats this kind of necessary efficacy as central to genuine causation.
The principle that preserving a creature in existence is, from God’s side, continuous with creating it, a principle used by occasionalists to argue against creaturely causal power.

questions_to_think_about: Does the possibility that God could prevent an effect show that a creature has no causal power, or only that its power is not absolute?
Can a cause be genuine without necessitating its effect?
Does continuous creation support occasionalism, or could it be understood as God’s preserving creatures while they still act?
Is regularity in nature enough for causation, or must there be an underlying necessary connection?
If physical events are caused by God but minds remain active, how should a philosopher explain freedom and responsibility?

summaries.example: Think about pressing a light switch. The light usually turns on right afterward. Most people say the switch causes the light to turn on. An occasionalist might say the switch’s movement is only an occasion: it gives God the situation in which God produces the light according to a regular rule. The switch is still part of the story, but it is not the true cause. Another philosopher might say the switch really does have causal power, while God keeps the switch and the electrical system in existence.
summaries.summary: Occasionalism is a philosophical theory about what causation really is. We normally describe events by saying that one thing causes another: fire causes water to heat, a ball causes another ball to move, or a decision causes an arm to rise. Occasionalists argue that this ordinary description may not reveal the deepest cause. In the strongest form of the theory, God is the only genuine cause. Created things have no causal power of their own. Instead, a created event can be an occasional cause: it is the situation in which God regularly brings about another event. This explains why nature can be orderly even if created things do not cause effects. Not every philosopher associated with occasionalism accepted exactly the same view. Global occasionalism denies all creaturely causation. Local occasionalism denies it only in a selected domain, such as interactions between bodies. The entry traces related ideas through Islamic philosophy, medieval Christian Europe, and early modern European philosophy. Al-Ghazali challenged the claim that created natures contain necessary connections to their effects. If fire and cotton were connected in a way that even God could not interrupt, miracles would appear impossible. However, interpreters disagree about whether al-Ghazali himself denied every form of creaturely causation. Nicholas of Autrecourt also criticized claims about necessary causal links, though he may have been a skeptic rather than an occasionalist. Among later thinkers, Descartes’s position is debated, while several Cartesians defended restricted or global forms of the theory. Malebranche became its most influential Western defender. key_ideas: Occasionalists question the everyday idea that one created thing directly causes another.
They still accept that nature has regular patterns. They explain those patterns through God’s regular activity.
Some occasionalists make the claim about all created things; others apply it only to certain kinds of events.
Al-Ghazali criticized the idea that created things must produce their effects, because this could seem to restrict divine power and leave no room for miracles.
Malebranche argued that bodies are passive and also developed arguments about knowledge, necessary connections, and God’s continuous creation.
Berkeley denied causal power to physical objects, but he considered spirits or minds active, so his position is not identical to Malebranche’s.
summaries.why_it_matters: Occasionalism matters because it makes us examine a familiar word—cause—in a careful way. It asks whether regular order, direct production, and dependence on God are the same thing or different things. Comparing occasionalism with conservationism and concurrentism shows that philosophers can agree that God is involved in nature while disagreeing about how much causal power belongs to created things. The debate also connects ideas about miracles, natural laws, mind-body interaction, and human agency.

important_terms.definition: A view about causation saying that God is the only genuine cause in a particular area, while created things are only occasions for effects.
The strongest version of occasionalism, which says that no created thing is a genuine cause anywhere.
A limited version of occasionalism, which denies created causation only in a chosen area, such as body-to-body events.
An event that regularly comes before another event and gives God the occasion to produce the later event, without producing it itself.
A cause that truly brings about its effect, rather than merely being regularly connected with it.
The view that God preserves created things, but creatures themselves directly produce ordinary natural effects.
The view that God and a creature both directly contribute to producing a natural effect.
The claim that one event must produce another because of the natures or powers of the things involved.

questions_to_think_about: If two events always occur together, must the first one cause the second?
Could a created cause be real even if God could stop it from producing its usual effect?
Why might someone think that miracles require natural causes not to be necessary?
What is the difference between God preserving a thing and God directly causing every change involving it?
